title: Nature's Treasures
intro: Air, water, soil, plants, animals, minerals — these are nature's treasures, and they all keep life on Earth going. This chapter shows where these treasures come from, why they matter, and what we can do to protect them.

sections.heading: What Are Natural Resources?
bullets: Anything we get from nature and use is a natural resource — air, water, soil, plants, animals, minerals.
Without these resources, no person, plant, or animal could live.
Some resources renew themselves quickly (sunlight, wind, water) — these are renewable.
Others form over thousands or millions of years (coal, oil, metals) — these are non-renewable.
How carefully we use a resource decides how long it will last for us and for future generations.

sections.heading: Air and Why It Matters
bullets: Air is a mixture of gases — mainly nitrogen, oxygen, a little carbon dioxide and water vapour.
All living things breathe oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.
Plants take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and release oxygen — they keep the air balanced.
Wind is moving air; it carries seeds, drives windmills, and helps spread rain clouds.
Smoke, dust, and harmful gases pollute the air; clean air is essential for healthy lungs.

sections.heading: Water and Where We Find It
bullets: Water covers most of Earth's surface — but most of it is salty seawater.
Fresh water comes from rivers, lakes, glaciers, rainfall, and groundwater wells.
Less than 1% of Earth's total water is fresh and easily usable.
We use water for drinking, cooking, washing, farming, factories, and producing electricity (hydropower).
Polluting water with sewage and chemicals harms us and other living things.

sections.heading: Soil and Land
bullets: Soil is the top layer of land where plants put down their roots.
It is made of bits of weathered rock, dead plant matter, water, air, and tiny living things.
Different soils suit different plants — sandy soil drains fast, clay soil holds water.
Soil takes hundreds of years to form but can be lost quickly through wind and rain (erosion).
Planting trees, terrace farming, and avoiding chemical overuse keep soil healthy.

sections.heading: Forests and Wildlife
bullets: Forests are large areas covered with trees, plants, and animals living together.
They give us wood, fruits, medicines, and many other useful things.
Forests release oxygen, hold soil with their roots, and help bring rain.
Wildlife — birds, mammals, reptiles, insects — live in forests and other habitats.
Cutting down trees (deforestation) and hunting wildlife reduce nature's balance.

sections.heading: Minerals and Fossil Fuels
bullets: Minerals are useful substances we dig out of the ground — iron, copper, aluminium, salt.
Iron and aluminium become tools, vehicles, buildings; copper becomes wires.
Coal, petroleum, and natural gas are fossil fuels — formed over millions of years from buried plants and animals.
We burn fossil fuels in power plants, vehicles, and stoves, but they release carbon dioxide and pollutants.
These resources are non-renewable — once used up, they take a very long time to form again.

sections.heading: Renewable Energy
bullets: Solar energy: sunlight captured by panels for electricity or hot water.
Wind energy: large windmills turn wind into electricity.
Hydropower: flowing water in dams turns turbines.
Biomass: dried plant matter and animal waste burned for energy.
Renewable sources don't run out and pollute much less than fossil fuels.

sections.heading: Conserving Nature's Treasures
bullets: Save water: close taps, fix leaks, water plants only when needed, harvest rainwater.
Save air: walk, cycle, or use public transport; avoid burning waste.
Save energy: switch off lights and fans; use efficient bulbs and appliances.
Reduce, reuse, recycle to cut down on waste sent to landfills.
Plant trees, protect forests, and respect wildlife.
Small daily actions add up across millions of people.

key_takeaways: Natural resources include air, water, soil, forests, wildlife, minerals, and fuels.
Renewable resources renew quickly (sunlight, wind); non-renewable ones (coal, oil, metals) form very slowly.
Plants and animals depend on clean air, water, and healthy soil.
Fossil fuels release pollution; renewable energy from sun, wind, and water is cleaner.
Forests give wood, oxygen, and homes to wildlife — protecting them protects life.
Conserving resources by saving water, energy, and reducing waste matters for everyone's future.

glossary.definition: Anything from nature that humans use, like water, soil, or minerals.
A resource that nature replaces quickly, like sunlight, wind, or growing plants.
A resource that takes a very long time to form, like coal or metals.
Coal, petroleum, or natural gas, formed from buried plants and animals over millions of years.
A useful natural substance dug out of the ground, like iron, copper, or salt.
Carefully using and protecting natural resources so they last.
The slow wearing away of soil or rock by wind, water, or ice.
Energy source from dried plant matter and animal waste.
Electricity made from the energy of moving water, often in dams.
The cutting down of large areas of forest.
